meta.title: Mermaid Sequence Diagram: Syntax and Examples
meta.description: How to write a mermaid sequence diagram: participants, arrow types, activation bars, loops, alt blocks and notes — with copy-paste examples.

card.title: Mermaid sequence diagrams
card.excerpt: Participants, arrow types, activation bars, loops and alt blocks — the whole sequence diagram syntax with runnable examples.

h1: How to write a mermaid sequence diagram
intro: A sequence diagram shows who talks to whom, in what order. In mermaid it takes about as long to write as it takes to describe out loud, which is why it is the diagram type that survives longest in a codebase. Everything below is copy-paste ready for the [editor](app:).

blocks.text: Declare the diagram type, then write one line per message. Participants are created on first mention, in the order they appear.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  User->>API: POST /orders
  API->>DB: INSERT order
  DB-->>API: order id
  API-->>User: 201 Created

blocks.text: Declare participants explicitly with `participant User` when you want a specific left-to-right order rather than the order of first mention.

rows: Async message — open arrowhead, no reply expected
Message that fails or is dropped

blocks.text: The convention worth keeping: **solid for the call, dashed for the return**. A reader can then tell a request from a response without reading a single label.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Browser
  participant A as API gateway
  participant S as Order service
  U->>A: GET /orders
  A->>S: list(userId)
  S-->>A: orders
  A-->>U: 200 OK

blocks.text: Use `actor U as Browser` instead of `participant` to draw a stick figure — worth it for the human at the left edge of an authentication flow.
Activation bars show how long a participant is busy. Either mark them explicitly with `activate`/`deactivate`, or append `+` and `-` to the arrows, which is shorter and harder to get out of balance.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  User->>+API: POST /pay
  API->>+Bank: charge
  Bank-->>-API: authorised
  API-->>-User: receipt

sequenceDiagram
  User->>API: POST /import
  loop every row
    API->>DB: upsert row
  end
  alt all rows valid
    API-->>User: 200 OK
  else some failed
    API-->>User: 422 with errors
  end
  par notify
    API->>Email: send summary
  and audit
    API->>Log: write entry
  end

items: `opt <label>` … `end` — a branch that may simply not happen.
`par <label>` … `and <label>` … `end` — things happening at the same time.
`critical` / `break` — a section that must not be interrupted, and an early exit.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram User->>API: POST /login Note right of API: Rate limited
5 per minute API-->>User: token Note over User,API: Token is valid for 30 days

blocks.text: `Note over A,B` spans two participants and is the right place for a constraint that belongs to the interaction rather than to either side of it.

blocks.caption: OAuth login, end to end.
blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  actor U as User
  participant A as App
  participant P as Provider
  U->>+A: Click "Sign in"
  A-->>-U: Redirect to provider
  U->>+P: Authorise
  P-->>-U: Redirect back with code
  U->>+A: GET /callback?code=…
  A->>+P: Exchange code for token
  P-->>-A: access token
  Note right of A: Session cookie set here
  A-->>-U: Signed in

blocks.heading: Edit this diagram
blocks.text: Paste it into the code tab and change a line — the preview redraws as you type.

items.q: How do I number the messages?
items.a: Put `autonumber` on the line right after `sequenceDiagram`. Every message then gets a sequential number, which makes a diagram much easier to talk about in review comments.

items.q: Can a participant send a message to itself?
items.a: Yes — write the same name on both sides: `API->>API: retry`. Mermaid draws the loop back into the same lifeline.

items.q: How do I show that a participant is destroyed?
items.a: Use `destroy <name>` before the message that ends it, or `create participant <name>` to have it appear mid-diagram rather than at the top.

items.q: Can I edit a sequence diagram on the visual canvas?
items.a: The visual canvas edits flowcharts. Sequence diagrams are written on the code tab, where they render live in the preview — which is usually faster anyway, since a sequence diagram is essentially a list of lines.
